chapterTitle: The Shrewd Manager, Mammon, and the Rich Man and Lazarus
themeTitle: What You Do With Mammon Becomes the Address You Keep Forever

scripture.text: He also said to his disciples, “There was a certain rich man who had a manager. An accusation was made to him that this man was wasting his possessions.
scripture.understanding: Jesus turns from the crowd to His disciples with an unsettling story. A rich man's estate-manager (oikonomos) is accused of squandering the very wealth entrusted to him — the opening move in a lesson about stewarding what is not your own.

scripture.text: He called him, and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an accounting of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
scripture.understanding: The master demands the books and fires him on the spot. The reckoning is the hinge of the parable — a day of accounting is coming when every steward must show what he did with another's goods.

scripture.text: “The manager said within himself, ‘What will I do, seeing that my lord is taking away the management position from me? I don’t have strength to dig. I am ashamed to beg.
scripture.understanding: Facing ruin, the manager talks to himself. Too soft for the ditch, too proud for the street — he must find a third way before the door of opportunity swings shut.

scripture.text: I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from management, they may receive me into their houses.’
scripture.understanding: He lands on his plan: use his last hours of authority to buy future welcome. He will trade a position he is losing for people who will owe him.

scripture.text: Calling each one of his lord’s debtors to him, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe to my lord?’
scripture.understanding: While he still holds the pen, he summons his master's debtors one at a time. The window is closing, so he moves fast to convert authority into relationships.

scripture.text: He said, ‘A hundred batos of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’
scripture.understanding: A hundred batos of olive oil — roughly eight hundred gallons — cut in half with the stroke of a reed pen. He is turning his master's wealth into personal goodwill that will outlast his job.

scripture.text: Then he said to another, ‘How much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
scripture.understanding: A hundred cors of wheat — a small fortune — discounted by a fifth. Each debtor now carries a debt of gratitude the manager intends to collect when he is jobless and homeless.

scripture.text: “His lord commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely, for the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light.
scripture.understanding: The shocking twist: the master praises the shrewdness (not the dishonesty) of the man he just fired. Jesus' point is a scalpel — worldly people are more strategic about their future than the children of light are about eternity.

scripture.text: I tell you, make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents.
scripture.understanding: Now the application: use money — 'unrighteous mammon' — to make eternal friends. Invest what will fail you into people and the Kingdom, so that when it runs out you are welcomed into everlasting dwellings.

scripture.text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
scripture.understanding: A law of the heart: faithfulness is measured not by the size of the trust but by the character of the trustee. How you handle a single dollar reveals how you would handle a fortune — or a soul.

scripture.text: If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
scripture.understanding: Money is the test, not the prize. If you cannot be trusted with mere mammon, God will not hand you 'the true riches' — the eternal treasures of His Kingdom.

scripture.text: If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?
scripture.understanding: Everything you now hold is 'another's' — it is God's, on loan, and you leave it all at the grave. Only what you receive by faithfulness becomes truly 'your own' in the age to come.

scripture.text: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to one, and despise the other. You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon.”
scripture.understanding: The verdict, with no middle ground: divided allegiance is impossible. One master will be loved, the other despised. Money makes a jealous god, and the true God will not share His throne.

scripture.text: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, also heard all these things, and they scoffed at him.
scripture.understanding: The Pharisees, literally 'lovers of silver' (philargyros), overhear and sneer. Jesus' teaching has exposed the idol hiding under their religious robes, and mockery is the reflex of an exposed heart.

scripture.text: He said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men, but God knows your hearts. For that which is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
scripture.understanding: Jesus strips the mask: they perform righteousness for human applause, but God reads the ledger of the heart. What the crowd exalts, God calls an abomination.

scripture.text: The law and the prophets were until John. From that time the Good News of God’s Kingdom is preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it.
scripture.understanding: A pivot in redemptive history: the era of Law and Prophets pointed forward to John the Baptist; now the Kingdom is being preached and people are pressing violently to get in. The age of fulfillment has broken open.

scripture.text: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one tiny stroke of a pen in the law to fall.
scripture.understanding: Yet the new age discards nothing of God's Law — not the smallest stroke of a letter. The Kingdom does not abolish God's righteous standard; it fulfills it to the last mark.

scripture.text: Everyone who divorces his wife, and marries another, commits adultery. He who marries one who is divorced from a husband commits adultery.
scripture.understanding: A concrete case of that unchanging standard, aimed at money-loving men who bent the Law to suit themselves: divorce-and-remarry is named plainly as adultery. God's covenant view of marriage is not softened by the new age.

scripture.text: “Now there was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, living in luxury every day.
scripture.understanding: The second parable opens. A nameless rich man dressed in royal purple and the finest linen feasts lavishly — not on feast days, but every single day. Luxury has become his entire way of life.

scripture.text: A certain beggar, named Lazarus, was taken to his gate, full of sores,
scripture.understanding: At his gate lies Lazarus — the only named character in any parable Jesus ever told — a beggar covered in open sores, carried and dumped like refuse at the threshold of another man's plenty. His name means 'God has helped.'

scripture.text: and desiring to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Yes, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
scripture.understanding: He longs merely for the scraps under the table; the only creatures who attend to him are the street dogs, licking his wounds. The rich man steps past this misery every day and does absolutely nothing.

scripture.text: The beggar died, and he was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died, and was buried.
scripture.understanding: Death, the great equalizer, comes for both. Angels personally carry the beggar to Abraham's side; the rich man simply 'was buried' — his purple and his feasts end abruptly in a hole in the ground.

scripture.text: In Hades, he lifted up his eyes, being in torment, and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus at his bosom.
scripture.understanding: The reversal is total and conscious. In Hades, in active torment (basanos), the rich man lifts his eyes and sees the very man he ignored now resting in honor at Abraham's side.

scripture.text: He cried and said, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue! For I am in anguish in this flame.’
scripture.understanding: Now the rich man begs — the tables turned — for a single drop of water from Lazarus's fingertip. Even in torment he still thinks of Lazarus as an errand-boy beneath him, and still knows his name.

scripture.text: “But Abraham said, ‘Son, remember that you, in your lifetime, received your good things, and Lazarus, in the same way, bad things. But here he is now comforted, and you are in anguish.
scripture.understanding: Abraham answers gently but finally: 'remember.' The accounts have been reversed. The rich man collected his good things on earth while ignoring the man at his gate; now comfort belongs to the one he despised.

scripture.text: Besides all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, that those who want to pass from here to you are not able, and that no one may cross over from there to us.’
scripture.understanding: And there is no appeal court: a great chasm (chasma) has been permanently 'fixed,' impassable in both directions. The choices of this life harden into the fixed geography of the next.

scripture.text: “He said, ‘I ask you therefore, father, that you would send him to my father’s house;
scripture.understanding: Losing all hope for himself, the rich man pleads for his living family — send Lazarus back as a messenger to his father's house.

scripture.text: for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, so they won’t also come into this place of torment.’
scripture.understanding: He has five brothers still living exactly as he lived. He begs for a resurrection-messenger to shock them out of their comfort before they land in this place of torment.

scripture.text: “But Abraham said to him, ‘They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them.’
scripture.understanding: Abraham's reply is the theological spine of the whole chapter: 'They have Moses and the prophets.' God's written Word is already the sufficient warning; the problem was never a lack of evidence, but a refusal to listen.

scripture.text: “He said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if one goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’
scripture.understanding: The rich man insists a spectacular miracle would succeed where Scripture failed — surely a ghost from the grave would make them repent (metanoeo). He still trusts sensation over the plain Word of God.

scripture.text: “He said to him, ‘If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.’”
scripture.understanding: Jesus' devastating conclusion: a heart that will not bow to the Scriptures it already has will not be persuaded even by a resurrection. It is a prophecy of His own empty tomb — and of the enemies who saw it and still would not believe.

visualMeditations.title: The Shrewd Steward's Last Hours
visualMeditations.image: Picture a man who has just been fired but the news is not yet public. He sits at a desk with the master's account scrolls spread before him, and one by one the debtors are hurried in. 'How much do you owe?' A hundred batos of oil — he snatches the bill and says, 'Sit down, quickly, write fifty.' A hundred cors of wheat — 'Write eighty.' His reed pen flies across the parchment while his authority is bleeding out by the minute, converting his master's wealth into a network of grateful friends who will owe him a roof.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is not a lesson in fraud; it is a lesson in foresight. The man saw the crisis coming and acted decisively with the resources still in his hand while there was still time to act. Jesus holds up the world's cleverness as a rebuke: the children of this age plan feverishly for a retirement that ends at the grave, while the children of light drift casually toward an eternity that never ends.

visualMeditations.title: A Table and a Gate
visualMeditations.image: On one side of a wall: a man draped in Tyrian purple and Egyptian linen, reclining at a groaning table, the smell of roasted meat and wine filling the air — and this is not a holiday, it is Tuesday, and Wednesday, and every day. On the other side of that same wall, at the gate he passes through morning and evening, lies Lazarus: skin broken open with running sores, too weak to wave off the street dogs that come to lick his wounds, staring at the crumbs that servants sweep off that table into the trash.
visualMeditations.meaning: The distance between heaven and hell was, in this life, the width of one gate that the rich man could have opened any day and never did. His sin was not that he was rich; his sin was that a dying man lay at his doorstep and he had trained himself not to see him. Comfort had made him blind, and blindness is the beginning of damnation.

visualMeditations.title: The Great Reversal — Two Deaths
visualMeditations.image: Two funerals. The beggar's body is likely thrown into a pauper's pit with no mourners — but unseen by human eyes, angels themselves descend and carry his soul, tenderly, to Abraham's bosom. The rich man dies too, and now there is a procession, a tomb, spices, weeping heirs — 'and was buried,' the parable says flatly, and stops. Then the camera cuts: the rich man opens his eyes in Hades, in flames, and lifts his gaze across an infinite distance to see the beggar he stepped over, resting at the father of the faithful.
visualMeditations.meaning: Everything the world could measure said the rich man had won and Lazarus had lost. Death reversed the verdict in an instant. The angels came for the beggar and the earth swallowed the tycoon, and every ranking the world had made was turned exactly upside down.

visualMeditations.title: The Fixed Chasm
visualMeditations.image: The rich man, screaming for a single drop of water, hears Abraham describe the terrain between them: a chasm — a vast, yawning canyon with no bridge, no rope, no path down one side or up the other. It is not merely wide; it is 'fixed,' set in place, permanent as the roots of the mountains. Lazarus cannot come to him with water; he cannot climb to Lazarus. The gate the rich man once could have crossed in three steps has become a gulf no one will ever cross again.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is the most sobering image in the chapter: the choices of this life do not stay soft forever. At death they set like concrete. Hell is real, conscious, and locked; there is no second reckoning, no purgatorial commute, no do-over. The time to open the gate is now, on this side of the chasm, because the chasm is fixed.

structure.label: The Parable of the Shrewd Manager (v. 1-8)
structure.body: A steward, about to be fired for waste, uses his final hours of authority to make friends for the future — and his master commends his shrewdness.

structure.label: The Lesson: Mammon or God (v. 9-13)
structure.body: Money is a test of faithfulness and a rival lord; you can invest it toward eternity, but you cannot serve it and God at the same time.

structure.label: The Pharisees Rebuked; the Kingdom and the Law (v. 14-18)
structure.body: The money-loving Pharisees scoff; Jesus exposes their self-justification, announces the arrival of the Kingdom, and affirms that not one stroke of God's Law falls.

structure.label: The Rich Man and Lazarus (v. 19-31)
structure.body: Two men, two deaths, a total reversal, a fixed chasm, and a final word: those who ignore Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by a resurrection.

sections.heading: The Scandal of the Shrewd Manager: Did Jesus Praise a Crook?
paragraphs: This is one of the most misread parables in the Gospels, and the discomfort is the whole point. A manager is fired for wasting his master's goods, and in his final hours he slashes the debts owed to his master — and then the master commends him. Did Jesus just endorse cooking the books? No. Read the text with precision: the master 'commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely' — he is praised for his phronimos (shrewd, sagacious foresight), not for his dishonesty. Jesus explicitly labels him the 'dishonest manager' in the same breath. The commendation is aimed at one thing only: the man grasped that his position was ending, and he acted decisively, with the resources still in his hand, to secure his future before the window closed.

That is the razor Jesus presses against His disciples: 'the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light.' The gambler, the schemer, the corporate climber will burn the midnight oil, take the risk, and spend every asset to secure a retirement that death will empty in a single night. The believer, who actually has an eternity to plan for, too often drifts — casual with time, casual with money, casual with the one commodity that can be converted into everlasting welcome. Jesus is not telling you to be dishonest; He is telling you to be at least as strategic about heaven as the world is about earth. Take your 'unrighteous mammon' — money, which is temporary and tainted and will certainly 'fail' — and convert it now, while you still hold it, into friends who will greet you in the eternal tents. Give it to the poor, pour it into the Kingdom, use it to seek and to save the lost, so that the wealth that dies with the world buys you a welcome in the world that never ends.

sections.heading: The Great Reversal and the Fixed Chasm: Two Parables, One Wound
paragraphs: The two parables of Luke 16 are not random neighbors; they are the same sword struck twice. The first says use mammon rightly or it will testify against you; the second shows a man who used it wrongly and now hears its testimony forever. Between them sit the scoffing Pharisees, 'lovers of money' (philargyros), who justified themselves before men while God read their hearts. The rich man of the second parable is their portrait: respectable, comfortable, religiously untroubled — and lost. Notice carefully what damns him. He is not condemned for a single named crime, no theft, no violence, no blasphemy. He is condemned for a gate he walked through twice a day past a dying man he never once helped. Comfort had anesthetized his compassion, and the failure to love was itself the verdict.

Then comes the chasm — 'a great gulf fixed' — the most solemn geography in Scripture. It teaches that death is not a pause but a door that locks behind you, and that the state of the soul at death is permanent and conscious: Lazarus consciously comforted, the rich man consciously in anguish, both fully aware, neither able to cross. There is no bargaining, no bridge, no drop of water. And the final exchange delivers the chapter's deepest truth: the rich man begs for a spectacular sign — send a man back from the dead! — and Abraham refuses, because the real problem was never insufficient evidence. 'They have Moses and the prophets.' The family already possessed the Word of God, and a heart that will not bow to the Scripture it already has will not be softened by a ghost. Miracles do not create faith in a rebellious heart; they only harden it further. What saves is not sensation but submission to the Word already given.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Verse 31 is one of the most breathtaking prophecies Jesus ever spoke, because He fulfilled it twice over. 'If they don't listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.' First, He proved it with a literal Lazarus. In John 11 Jesus raised a real man named Lazarus from the tomb after four days — a resurrection witnessed by crowds — and the response of the religious leaders was not repentance but murder: 'So from that day forward they took counsel that they might put him to death' (John 11:53), and 'the chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also' (John 12:10). A man rose from the dead, and they schemed to send him back. The parable came true in front of their eyes.

Second, and greater, Jesus fulfilled it in His own resurrection. The very leaders who demanded signs saw the empty tomb reported to them and, exactly as verse 31 predicted, bribed the guards and refused to be persuaded (Matthew 28:11-15). One did rise from the dead, and they were not persuaded. And the money that opens this chapter finds its verdict in Paul's warning to Timothy: the Pharisees were 'lovers of money' (philargyros, v. 14), and Paul writes, 'For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows' (1 Timothy 6:10). Luke 16 shows you the piercing in full: a rich man in flames, begging for water, pierced forever by the mammon he chose over God.

lexicon.insight: Literally a 'house-law-keeper' (oikos, house + the base of nomos, law) — the manager of another man's estate, who controls the wealth but owns none of it. This single word carries the whole chapter: you are not an owner, you are an oikonomos. Everything in your hands — money, time, gifts, breath — belongs to Another, and a day of accounting is fixed. The question is never 'how much is mine?' but 'how faithful was I with what was never mine?'

A word of Aramaic origin meaning wealth, riches, or property — but rooted in the idea of 'that in which one trusts.' Jesus deliberately personifies it as a rival deity ('you cannot serve God and Mammon'), spelling it as a name, a master with a throne. Mammon is not merely cash; it is money the moment it becomes an object of confidence and worship. It promises security and demands your soul in payment, and it will 'fail' (v. 9) at exactly the moment you need it most — the hour of death.

The adverb from phronimos, meaning prudently, sagaciously, with foresight and cautious calculation. This is the precise hinge of the first parable: the master commends the manager not for being honest (he was not) but for acting phronimos — for reading the future accurately and moving decisively before the door shut. Jesus is not baptizing his ethics; He is envying his urgency and asking why the sons of light are not at least this shrewd about eternity.

A compound of philos (loving, fond) and argyros (silver) — literally 'silver-lovers.' Luke uses this exact word to diagnose the Pharisees, and it is the same disease Paul names in 1 Timothy 6:10. It exposes the tragedy of the whole chapter: religion and greed can live in the same heart, quoting Scripture with one hand while clutching silver with the other. Their scoffing was not a theological objection; it was the wince of an idol being named out loud.

From a root meaning to 'gape' or 'yawn' — a chasm, an impassable interval, a vacancy that cannot be bridged. It is described as 'fixed' (perfect tense: set in place and remaining so). This is the most solemn word in Luke 16. It teaches that eternity is not fluid: at death the soul's condition is sealed, conscious, and permanent, with no crossing in either direction. The gate the rich man could have crossed in life became the chasm no one crosses in death — and the only side of it you can choose from is this one.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with the one idol most respectable believers never repent of — money — and the terrifying permanence of how we treat the people God places at our gate.

items.title: Whose Steward Are You?
items.body: Before God ever asks how much you gave, He asks a prior question: do you even know you are a steward and not an owner? The manager's whole crisis began when he forgot the wealth was not his. Everything in your possession right now — your salary, your phone, your talents, the hours of this very week — is entrusted, not owned, and an accounting is coming that you cannot postpone. So look honestly: are you managing God's resources as a faithful steward preparing to give an account, or spending them as an owner who thinks the reckoning will never come? If your Master called for the books today, what would they say about you?

items.title: The Master You Actually Serve
items.body: Jesus says it flatly: you cannot serve two masters. Not 'you shouldn't' — you cannot. One will be loved and the other despised, and self-deception is the specialty of the money-loving heart. Here is the diagnostic: what makes you feel secure, what you lie awake protecting, what you cannot imagine surrendering — that is your master. The Pharisees were certain they served God, right up until Jesus said the thing they exalted was 'an abomination in the sight of God.' Do not assume you are free of Mammon just because you are not wealthy; a poor man can worship money as desperately as a rich one. Which master's voice do you actually obey when the two of them give opposite commands?

items.title: The Lazarus at Your Gate
items.body: The rich man went to torment not for a scandalous crime but for a daily blindness — he stepped over a dying man so many times that he stopped seeing him. God has almost certainly placed a Lazarus at your gate: a person, a need, a suffering you pass regularly and have trained yourself not to notice. The chasm in the next life was the width of one gate in this one. So the Spirit asks with piercing directness: who is lying at your gate right now that you have learned to walk past? And is the reason you cannot see him that your own table is simply too full?

audit.title: The Ownership Audit
audit.body: Do you live as an owner or as a steward? Name the three possessions you would fight hardest to keep. Now ask: would you release any of them the instant God asked? If the answer catches in your throat, you have found where you have quietly moved from managing God's wealth to owning your own.

audit.title: The Two-Masters Test
audit.body: When a financial decision and an obedience collide — a tithe you feel you cannot afford, a dishonest gain you could easily take, a generous gift that would cost you comfort — which master wins? Track your last three money decisions honestly. They are a more accurate confession of who you serve than anything you sang on Sunday.

audit.title: The Gate Check
audit.body: Who is the Lazarus you walk past? Name the specific person or need at your gate that you have grown numb to — the relative, the coworker, the neighbor, the ministry you keep meaning to help. What exactly have you done for them in the last month, and what has your full table cost you the ability to see?

practices.title: Convert Mammon Into Eternal Friends
practices.body: This week, make one deliberate, costly transfer of 'unrighteous mammon' into eternity. Choose an amount that you will actually feel, and give it directly to a poor person or a Kingdom work that seeks and saves the lost — not your normal budgeted giving, but an extra, sacrificial act. As you give, say aloud: 'I am sending this ahead. When it fails, may this welcome me into the eternal tents.'

practices.title: Open One Gate
practices.body: Identify your Lazarus by name today, and this week take one concrete step to open the gate you have been walking past. Not money necessarily — presence. Visit them, feed them, sit with them, learn their name and their story the way the rich man never learned Lazarus's need. Put it on the calendar now with a day and a time, because a gate you intend to open 'someday' is a chasm forming in slow motion.

prayerReflection: “Father, You know my heart the way You knew the Pharisees' — so I will not justify myself before You today. I confess that I have too often lived as an owner when I am only a steward, clutching Your resources as if the accounting would never come. Break the grip of Mammon in me; I refuse to bow to the silver that promises security and demands my soul. Teach me the shrewdness of the manager without his dishonesty — to act now, decisively, with what is still in my hand, sending my treasure ahead into the eternal tents. Open my eyes to the Lazarus at my gate, the one I have trained myself not to see, and give me the compassion I have withheld. And Lord, guard me from the deadliest sin of that rich man — a heart that would not believe Your Word even if the dead rose. I have Moses and the prophets; I have the risen Christ; let me listen, and repent, and obey while the chasm is not yet fixed. Make me faithful in the very little, that You may trust me with the true riches. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Rich Fool
storyConnections.summary: Just four chapters earlier, Jesus told of a rich man whose land produced so abundantly that he tore down his barns to build bigger ones, telling his soul, 'take your ease, eat, drink, be merry.' God said, 'You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you.' He is the twin of the rich man in Luke 16 — a man who stored everything for himself and 'is not rich toward God.' Both men prove that a full barn and a full table are no defense at all against the night the soul is demanded, and that treasure hoarded for self is treasure lost forever.

storyConnections.title: The Rich Young Ruler
storyConnections.summary: Two chapters later, a good, moral, religious ruler asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life. Jesus names the one master he cannot serve alongside God: 'Sell all that you have... You will have treasure in heaven.' The man 'became very sad, for he was very rich,' and walked away. He is the living demonstration of Luke 16:13 — a man who, forced to choose between God and Mammon, chose Mammon and grieved. He could not make friends of unrighteous mammon because he could not loosen his fingers from it.

storyConnections.title: Zacchaeus the Tax Collector
storyConnections.summary: Then comes the glorious counter-example. A chief tax collector — a professional handler of unrighteous mammon — meets Jesus, and salvation walks into his house. Zacchaeus stands and says, 'Half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.' This is Luke 16:9 lived out perfectly: he took his tainted mammon and made eternal friends of the poor with it. Jesus declares, 'Today, salvation has come to this house,' and the very next words are the theme of the whole Gospel: 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.' The rich man of Luke 16 lifted his eyes in torment; Zacchaeus climbed down from his tree into life.
